reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign proliferation of small glands in and around the verumontanum, important chiefly as a histological mimic of low-grade prostatic adenocarcinoma
It is usually an incidental finding on needle biopsy, transurethral resection specimens or at autopsy, without specific symptoms
It is characterised by small crowded acini that retain a basal cell layer, which distinguishes it from carcinoma
It is commonly associated with corpora amylacea and lacks the infiltrative growth, nuclear enlargement and prominent nucleoli of cancer
It sits among the benign entities that can mimic malignancy in the prostate and posterior urethra, underlining the importance of careful histological interpretation when PSA is raised
Immunohistochemistry for basal cell markers confirms the benign nature
No treatment is required once malignancy has been excluded
reference.pathophysiology: Verumontanum mucosal gland hyperplasia is a benign hyperplastic proliferation of the small mucosal glands at the verumontanum in the posterior prostatic urethra. The closely packed small acini can architecturally resemble low-grade adenocarcinoma, but the retained basal cell layer, bland cytology and characteristic distinctive orange-brown luminal concretions mark the process as benign.
additionalDifferentials: Nephrogenic adenoma of the prostatic urethra
additionalInvestigations: Histopathological assessment by an experienced uropathologist
Immunohistochemistry for basal cell markers (p63, high-molecular-weight cytokeratin) and AMACR
Correlation with the anatomical site around the verumontanum
Multiparametric MRI if imaging correlation is needed
Repeat or targeted biopsy only if malignancy remains a genuine concern
redFlags: Coexisting atypical or malignant foci on the same specimen
A persistently rising PSA prompting further evaluation
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring specialist pathology review
reference.prognosis: Excellent; the lesion is entirely benign with no malignant potential, and its principal significance lies in avoiding a mistaken diagnosis of carcinoma.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing carcinoma on small crowded benign glands and prompting unnecessary treatment
Failing to use basal cell immunostains to confirm benignity
Attributing PSA elevation solely to this lesion without appropriate follow-up
Not seeking specialist review in equivocal cases
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
